0.title: Church History in Depth
0.essay:
The shorter Church History study tells the story in eight broad strokes. This one slows down. It gives more of the context: the politics, the controversies, the people and the dates. It shows why things happened as they did, and what the church learnt, often painfully, along the way.

Why go deeper?

The broad story can make the past look tidy. In fact, every creed was hammered out in conflict, every reform cost someone dearly, and every revival was mixed with error. Seeing the detail guards us against two mistakes. One is to think the church has always been pure, so that we copy the past without thought. The other is to think the church has always been corrupt, so that we ignore what God has taught his people over twenty centuries.

Above all, the detail shows the faithfulness of Christ. He promised, “I will build my church, and the gates of hell shall not prevail against it” (Matthew 16:18). History is the record of that promise kept, through emperors, plagues, schisms and the failures of the church itself.

The chapters

1. The World of the First Christians: Rome, Israel and the spread of the gospel. 2. Martyrs, Heretics and the Canon: the second and third centuries. 3. Constantine, Monks and Councils: from 313 to 451. 4. East and West Part Ways: from about 500 to 1100. 5. The High and Late Middle Ages: popes, friars, scholars and plague. 6. Before the Reformation: Waldensians, Wycliffe, Hus and the printing press. 7. Luther and the German Reformation. 8. Zwingli, the Anabaptists and Calvin. 9. Reformation in Britain: from Tyndale to 1689. 10. Rome’s Answer and the Age of Orthodoxy: Trent, the wars of religion and Dort. 11. Enlightenment, Revival and Missions. 12. Liberalism, Its Opponents and the Global Church: from 1800 to today.

How to read it

Read it with the shorter study, or on its own. Dates are given to help you place things, not to be memorised. Ask of each chapter three questions: What did God do? What did his people get right? Where did they go wrong, and are we in danger of the same?

For reflection

What do you already know of the church’s story? Where might your own picture of the past be too tidy, or too dark?

1.title: The World of the First Christians (c. AD 30–100)
1.essay:
The gospel did not arrive in an empty world. It came “when the fullness of time had come” (Galatians 4:4), into a world God had prepared: Roman roads, the Greek language, and Jewish communities scattered across the Mediterranean.

Rome

By the time of Jesus the Roman Empire stretched from Britain to Syria. Augustus (ruled 27 BC to AD 14) brought an end to civil war, and the Pax Romana, the Roman peace, made travel safer than it had been for centuries. Roman roads and sea routes carried Paul from Antioch to Rome. Roman law gave him rights as a citizen, which he used more than once (Acts 16:37; 22:25).

But Rome was also religious. Every city had its gods, and loyalty to the empire was shown by honouring them and, increasingly, the emperor. Christians who refused were seen not just as odd but as dangerous, enemies of the gods who kept the city safe.

The Greek world

Alexander the Great (died 323 BC) had spread Greek language and culture across the East. So a common Greek, called koine, was spoken from Spain to Egypt. The New Testament was written in it, and could be read almost everywhere. Greek philosophy also prepared questions the gospel would answer: What is the world made of? Is there one God? What is the good life? Paul spoke to Stoic and Epicurean philosophers in Athens (Acts 17:18).

The Jewish world

Judaism was the soil in which the church grew. Most Jews by now lived outside the land of Israel, in what is called the diaspora. They had synagogues in nearly every city, and their Scriptures had been translated into Greek, the version called the Septuagint. Around the synagogues gathered “God-fearers”, Gentiles drawn to the one God but not fully converted. Paul usually began in the synagogue, and many of his first Gentile converts came from this circle (Acts 13:16, 26).

Within the land there were several parties: Pharisees, Sadducees, Essenes and Zealots. Jesus clashed with each in different ways. Their hopes for a political Messiah help explain why so many rejected a crucified one.

How the gospel spread

Acts traces the movement Jesus foretold: “you will be my witnesses in Jerusalem and in all Judea and Samaria, and to the end of the earth” (Acts 1:8). After Stephen’s death, persecution scattered believers, and “those who were scattered went about preaching the word” (Acts 8:4). Antioch became the first great Gentile church and the base for Paul’s journeys. By about AD 60 there were churches in Asia Minor, Greece and Rome itself.

It was not only apostles who spread it. Merchants, soldiers, slaves and families carried the faith along the trade routes. Christians stood out for their care of the poor and sick, their faithfulness in marriage, and their refusal to abandon unwanted babies, a common practice in the Roman world.

The first persecutions

In AD 64 a great fire destroyed much of Rome. The historian Tacitus tells us that Nero blamed the Christians and had many put to death in horrible ways. Tradition holds that Peter and Paul were both killed in Rome in these years. In AD 70 the Romans destroyed Jerusalem and its temple, as Jesus had foretold (Luke 21:20–24). This ended the temple sacrifices and helped separate the church clearly from Judaism.

Near the end of the century, under the emperor Domitian, John was exiled to Patmos, where he received the Revelation. By AD 100 the apostles had died, but the churches they planted remained, and the writings they left became the New Testament.

For today

God prepared the world for the gospel long before anyone saw it. He still does. The roads, languages and networks of our day, from global English to the internet, can carry the gospel too. And the first Christians spread their faith less by programmes than by ordinary people living distinctively and speaking of Christ where they were.

For reflection

Where has God placed you along the “roads” of your own world, at work, online or in your neighbourhood, and who might hear the gospel through you?

2.title: Martyrs, Heretics and the Canon (c. AD 100–300)
2.essay:
In the two centuries after the apostles the church had no buildings to speak of, no legal standing and no Christian emperor. It faced outward pressure from persecution and inward pressure from false teaching. Out of both came a clearer grasp of the faith.

Why Christians were hated

Pagans accused Christians of atheism, because they rejected the gods. They accused them of cannibalism, because they spoke of eating Christ’s body, and of immorality, because they called one another brother and sister and met in secret. Above all, they were blamed for disasters. Tertullian, writing around 197, complained that if the Tiber flooded or the rains failed, the cry went up at once: “The Christians to the lion!”

Persecution in this period was mostly local and occasional. A governor might act if someone accused a Christian. Around 112 the emperor Trajan told Pliny, governor of Bithynia, not to hunt Christians down, but to punish them if they were accused and refused to offer sacrifice.

The martyrs

Ignatius, bishop of Antioch, was taken to Rome around 110 to be thrown to the beasts. On the way he wrote seven letters to churches, urging unity around their bishops and warning against false teaching. Polycarp, bishop of Smyrna and a disciple of John, was burned around 155. Told to curse Christ, he answered that he had served him eighty-six years, and Christ had done him no wrong. Perpetua, a young mother, and her slave Felicity died in the arena at Carthage in 203.

Then persecution became empire-wide. In 250 the emperor Decius ordered everyone to sacrifice and obtain a certificate to prove it. Many died, many fled, and many gave in. The worst persecution came under Diocletian, beginning in 303: churches were destroyed, Scriptures burned and leaders imprisoned.

The lapsed

Persecution raised a painful question. What should be done with those who denied Christ under pressure and then wanted to return? Some, like Novatian in Rome, said they could never be restored. Cyprian, bishop of Carthage (died 258), argued that they could be restored after real repentance. Later, after Diocletian, the Donatists in North Africa insisted that clergy who had handed over Scriptures were no longer valid ministers. The church as a whole rejected this. The worth of the sacraments rests on Christ, not on the purity of the minister.

The heresies

Gnosticism was the most serious threat. It taught that the material world was evil, made by a lesser god, and that salvation came through secret knowledge. So Christ could not truly have taken a body or died. John had already warned against those who deny “that Jesus Christ has come in the flesh” (1 John 4:2).

Marcion, around 140, rejected the God of the Old Testament as harsh and inferior, and kept only an edited Luke and ten of Paul’s letters. Montanism, from the 150s, claimed new prophecies from the Spirit that went beyond the apostles, and called for ever stricter rules.

The answer: Irenaeus and the rule of faith

Irenaeus of Lyons, writing Against Heresies around 180, answered the Gnostics. He argued that the true faith was public, not secret. It was taught openly by the apostles and handed down in the churches they founded. He summed it up in a “rule of faith”, a short statement of belief in one God the Father, Creator of all, in Christ his Son who became flesh for our salvation, and in the Holy Spirit. Such summaries became the seed of the creeds. Irenaeus also showed that the whole Bible tells one story, as God recovers in Christ what was lost in Adam.

The canon

Marcion’s edited Bible forced the church to say clearly which books were Scripture. The church did not create the canon. It recognised books that bore the marks of apostolic authority and were already received and read in the churches. By around 200 the four Gospels, Acts and Paul’s letters were accepted almost everywhere. A few books, such as Hebrews, James, 2 Peter and Revelation, took longer to be accepted everywhere. In 367 Athanasius listed the twenty-seven books of our New Testament, and councils in North Africa confirmed them in 393 and 397.

For today

The church of the martyrs teaches us what it costs to confess that Jesus, not Caesar, is Lord. It also teaches us that heresy usually begins with a reasonable-sounding idea: that the body does not matter, that the Old Testament God is too severe, or that the Spirit is saying something new. The answer then and now is the same: the public, apostolic word, read as one story.

For reflection

Polycarp had served Christ for eighty-six years. What would it take for you to remain faithful if confessing Christ cost you your job or your freedom?

3.title: Constantine, Monks and Councils (AD 313–451)
3.essay:
In a single generation the church went from the arena to the palace. It was a great relief, and a great danger. These years also produced the creeds that still define the Christian faith.

Constantine

In 312 Constantine defeated his rival at the Milvian Bridge outside Rome. He later said he had seen a sign of the cross with the words, “In this sign, conquer.” In 313, with his fellow emperor Licinius, he granted freedom of worship to Christians and restored their property, a policy often called the Edict of Milan.

How sincere was his faith? Historians still debate it. He kept some pagan titles and was baptised only on his deathbed in 337. But he favoured the church: he built churches, gave bishops legal powers and made Sunday a day of rest. Then in 380 the emperor Theodosius made Christianity the official religion of the empire.

Gain and loss

The gains were real. Persecution ended. Christians could worship openly, and the church could care for the poor on a large scale. But now it was an advantage to be a Christian. Crowds joined who had little faith. Emperors interfered in doctrine and in the choice of bishops. And in time, the church that had been persecuted began, sadly, to use the power of the state against heretics and pagans.

The monks

Partly in reaction, some Christians withdrew from the comfortable church into the desert. Antony of Egypt (died 356) gave away his property and lived as a hermit, and his life, written by Athanasius, inspired thousands. Pachomius organised monks into communities. Basil of Caesarea wrote rules for monastic life that joined prayer with care for the sick and poor. In the West, Benedict of Nursia (died about 547) wrote the Rule that shaped monasteries for a thousand years, balancing prayer, work and study.

The monks kept learning alive, copied Scripture and served the needy. But monasticism also spread the idea of two levels of Christians: the spiritual few and the ordinary many. The Reformers would later reject this.

Nicaea, 325

Around 318 Arius, a priest in Alexandria, began teaching that the Son was the first and greatest creature: “there was when he was not.” The dispute spread so widely that Constantine called the first worldwide council at Nicaea in 325. About 300 bishops affirmed that the Son is “of one substance” (homoousios) with the Father, true God from true God.

Nicaea did not end the controversy. For fifty years emperors swung between sides. Athanasius, bishop of Alexandria, was exiled five times for refusing to give way, and his stand gave rise to the phrase Athanasius contra mundum, Athanasius against the world. His argument was simple: only God can save us, so if the Son is not fully God, we are not saved.

Constantinople, 381

Three theologians from Cappadocia, Basil, his brother Gregory of Nyssa and their friend Gregory of Nazianzus, helped the church find words for the Trinity: one being (ousia) in three persons (hypostases). They also defended the full deity of the Holy Spirit. The Council of Constantinople in 381 expanded the Nicene Creed, confessing the Spirit as “the Lord, the giver of life, who with the Father and the Son is worshipped and glorified.” This is the Nicene Creed most churches recite today.

Ephesus and Chalcedon

The next question was how Christ can be both God and man. Nestorius, bishop of Constantinople, seemed to divide Christ into two persons, and objected to calling Mary “God-bearer” (Theotokos). Cyril of Alexandria opposed him, and the Council of Ephesus in 431 condemned Nestorius. Then Eutyches went to the other extreme, teaching that Christ’s humanity was swallowed up by his deity.

In 451 the Council of Chalcedon, guided by a letter from Pope Leo I known as Leo’s Tome, confessed one Christ “in two natures, without confusion, without change, without division, without separation.” It did not explain the mystery. It fenced it, ruling out the errors on every side. Some churches in Egypt, Syria and Armenia did not accept Chalcedon, and they remain separate today.

Augustine

Augustine of Hippo (354–430) stands over this age in the West. His Confessions told the story of his conversion. His battle with Pelagius, who taught that people can obey God without inward grace, led him to set out the doctrines of grace that the Reformers would later recover. And as Rome fell to the Goths in 410, he wrote The City of God, reminding Christians that no earthly empire is the kingdom of God.

For today

The creeds were not dry formulas. People were exiled and died for single words, because the words protected the gospel. And Constantine’s age is a warning to every church that gains influence: power can do great good, but it easily corrupts, and a church that is comfortable soon fills with people who do not know Christ.

For reflection

Would you be willing to stand alone, like Athanasius, for a truth about Christ that the majority around you had abandoned?

4.title: East and West Part Ways (c. AD 500–1100)
4.essay:
As the Western empire fell apart, the church became the strongest institution in Europe. Meanwhile the East went its own way, Islam swept across the old Christian lands, and in 1054 the great split between East and West became official.

The fall of the West

In 476 the last Western emperor was removed. Tribes such as the Goths, Franks and Lombards ruled the old provinces. In the chaos, bishops were often the only leaders left who could feed the hungry, negotiate with invaders and keep order. The bishop of Rome gained particular weight, because Rome was the city of Peter and Paul and the old capital.

Gregory the Great

Gregory I, pope from 590 to 604, organised food for Rome during famine and plague, and negotiated with the Lombards. He wrote a much-loved book on pastoral care. In 597 he sent Augustine (not the Augustine of Hippo) to evangelise the Anglo-Saxons in England. Gregory called himself “the servant of the servants of God”, yet in his time the papacy took on more and more power, laying the ground for the claims of later popes.

Celtic missions

Meanwhile, the faith was spreading from the British Isles. Patrick, a Briton captured as a boy by Irish raiders, returned to Ireland as a missionary in the fifth century. Columba founded a monastery on the island of Iona in 563, from which missionaries went to Scotland and northern England. Later, Boniface, an Englishman, took the gospel to the Germans and was martyred in 754.

The rise of Islam

Muhammad died in 632. Within a hundred years Arab armies had conquered Syria, Palestine, Egypt, North Africa and Spain. These were among the oldest Christian lands, the homes of Athanasius, Augustine and Cyril. Christians under Muslim rule were usually allowed to worship, but they paid a special tax and faced many restrictions, and over centuries most of their communities shrank. In 732 the Franks under Charles Martel stopped the Muslim advance into France at the Battle of Tours.

Charlemagne

On Christmas Day 800, Pope Leo III crowned Charlemagne, king of the Franks, as emperor in the West. This was the beginning of what became the Holy Roman Empire. Charlemagne encouraged learning, schools and the copying of manuscripts. But he also forced the Saxons to be baptised at the point of the sword, a grim example of mixing the kingdom of Christ with the power of the state.

Two churches drifting apart

East and West had long been different. The East spoke Greek, the West Latin. The East looked to the emperor in Constantinople, the West increasingly to the pope. They also argued over icons. The Second Council of Nicaea in 787 approved the veneration of images, after a long struggle in the East.

The deepest doctrinal dispute concerned the Holy Spirit. The Nicene Creed said the Spirit “proceeds from the Father.” In the West, the words “and the Son” (in Latin, filioque) were added, first in Spain in 589, and later accepted at Rome. The East objected, both to the theology and to the West changing a shared creed on its own.

In 1054 the pope’s legate laid a document on the altar of the great church in Constantinople, excommunicating its patriarch, who answered in kind. The split, called the Great Schism, hardened over the following centuries. It became bitter when Western crusaders sacked Constantinople in 1204.

The Crusades

In 1095 Pope Urban II called on Western knights to free Jerusalem and help the Eastern Christians. The First Crusade took Jerusalem in 1099 with terrible slaughter. Later crusades largely failed. Many crusaders were sincere, and the Muslim conquests they responded to were real. But the idea that fighting a holy war could earn forgiveness of sins was a serious distortion of the gospel.

For today

These centuries remind us that the gospel is not tied to any land. The church of North Africa, once the strongest in the world, almost vanished. The faith moved north and west, and now south and east again. They also show how easily the cross can be confused with the sword. Christ said, “My kingdom is not of this world” (John 18:36). His kingdom spreads by the word and the Spirit, not by force.

For reflection

Where are you tempted to advance Christ’s cause by worldly power or pressure, rather than by truth, love and prayer?

5.title: The High and Late Middle Ages (c. AD 1050–1450)
5.essay:
These centuries built the cathedrals and the universities, and produced some of the finest minds the church has known. They also saw the papacy reach the height of its power, and then fall into scandal. By the end, many longed for reform.

Reform from within

By the tenth century much of the church was in the hands of local lords who sold church offices and appointed relatives. A reform movement began at the monastery of Cluny, founded in 910, and spread. Pope Gregory VII (1073–1085) fought to free the church from lay control, insisting that only the church could appoint bishops. This led to the Investiture Controversy with the emperor Henry IV, who in 1077 stood barefoot in the snow at Canossa to beg the pope’s forgiveness.

The papacy at its height

Innocent III (1198–1216) claimed that the pope stood over kings as the sun over the moon. He placed whole kingdoms, including England, under interdict, closing their churches. In 1215 he called the Fourth Lateran Council, which defined transubstantiation (the teaching that the bread and wine become the body and blood of Christ in substance) and required every Christian to confess to a priest at least once a year. In 1302 Boniface VIII declared that submission to the pope was necessary for salvation.

The friars

Francis of Assisi (died 1226) gave up his wealth to live in poverty, preaching and caring for the poor. Dominic (died 1221) founded an order of preachers to teach sound doctrine. These friars took the faith into the growing towns. But the Dominicans also came to run much of the Inquisition, set up in the 1230s to root out heresy, which used torture and handed the condemned to the state to be burned.

The schools

Universities arose at Bologna, Paris and Oxford around 1200. Here theology was taught by the method called scholasticism: posing questions, weighing arguments and answering them carefully. Anselm of Canterbury (died 1109) had already written Why God Became Man, showing that Christ’s death satisfied the honour of God. Peter Lombard’s Sentences (around 1150) became the standard textbook. Thomas Aquinas (1225–1274) brought Aristotle’s philosophy into the service of theology in his vast Summa Theologiae.

The schoolmen were often brilliant, and the Reformers learnt from them. But theology increasingly became a matter of philosophy and church tradition, while the plain teaching of Scripture was buried.

The gospel obscured

Ordinary people heard Mass in Latin, which they did not understand. They were taught that grace came through the seven sacraments, that sins after baptism had to be paid for by penance here or in purgatory hereafter, and that the saints and Mary could help them. Indulgences, which reduced time in purgatory, were increasingly sold for money. The good news that a sinner is justified freely by faith in Christ was rarely heard clearly.

Captivity and schism

In 1309 the papacy moved to Avignon in France, where it stayed until 1377 under heavy French influence. Critics called it the Babylonian Captivity of the church. Soon after it returned to Rome, rival popes were elected, and from 1378 to 1417 there were two, and for a time three, popes, each excommunicating the others. The Council of Constance ended the Great Schism in 1417, and some hoped that councils, not popes, would now reform the church. But the popes soon reasserted their power.

The Black Death

From 1347 to 1351 plague killed perhaps a third of Europe’s people. Many priests died or fled. People were confronted with death on every side, and religious feeling grew intense, sometimes in strange forms such as bands of flagellants whipping themselves in public. The church’s hold was shaken, and many began to ask whether its rituals could really save.

For today

The medieval church shows that great learning and beautiful worship cannot make up for a hidden gospel. It also shows the danger of human power in the church. When an institution claims an authority that belongs to Christ and his word, it will sooner or later abuse it. “There is one God, and there is one mediator between God and men, the man Christ Jesus” (1 Timothy 2:5).

For reflection

What in your own church life could, over time, crowd out the plain message of grace through faith in Christ?

6.title: Before the Reformation (c. 1170–1517)
6.essay:
The Reformation did not come from nowhere. For three centuries before Luther, there were voices calling the church back to Scripture, and God was preparing the tools that would carry their message.

The Waldensians

Around 1170 Peter Waldo, a merchant of Lyons, paid for parts of the Bible to be translated into the local language, gave away his wealth and began preaching. His followers, the Waldensians, insisted that every Christian should hear Scripture and that the church must be judged by it. They were condemned and persecuted, and fled to the valleys of the Alps, where they survived for centuries. In 1532 they joined the Reformed churches.

John Wycliffe

John Wycliffe (around 1330–1384) was the leading theologian at Oxford. He taught that Scripture is the supreme authority over popes and councils, that the true church is the company of the elect, and that transubstantiation was unscriptural. He sent out preachers, later called Lollards, and inspired the first complete translation of the Bible into English, made from the Latin. He has been called the Morning Star of the Reformation. He died in his bed, but in 1428 his bones were dug up, burned and thrown into a river.

Jan Hus

Wycliffe’s writings reached Bohemia, where Jan Hus (around 1372–1415) preached in Prague in the Czech language. He attacked the sale of indulgences and taught that Christ, not the pope, is the head of the church. Summoned to the Council of Constance under a promise of safe conduct, he was arrested, condemned and burned in 1415. His followers, the Hussites, resisted for decades, and one branch became the Unity of the Brethren, ancestors of the later Moravians.

Savonarola

In Florence, the Dominican friar Girolamo Savonarola preached fiery sermons against corruption in the church and the city. He was executed in 1498. He was not an evangelical in the full sense, but his call for repentance showed how widely men longed for reform.

The Renaissance and Erasmus

The Renaissance revived the study of ancient languages and texts. Its motto was ad fontes, back to the sources. Christian humanists applied it to the Bible and the early fathers. Lorenzo Valla showed in 1440 that the Donation of Constantine, a document used to support papal claims to power, was a forgery.

The greatest of these scholars was Erasmus of Rotterdam. In 1516 he published the first printed Greek New Testament, with a fresh Latin translation. It showed that the Latin Bible the church used was wrong in places. For example, Jesus’ call to “repent” had been rendered in a way that suggested “do penance.” Erasmus mocked corrupt monks and popes. He never left the Roman church, and later he and Luther clashed over free will. But it was said that Erasmus laid the egg that Luther hatched.

The printing press

Around 1450 Johannes Gutenberg developed printing with movable type in Mainz. His first great book was a Latin Bible. Within decades presses had spread across Europe. Books became cheaper, and ideas spread faster than any council or inquisition could stop them. Within a few weeks of 1517, Luther’s theses were being read across Germany.

The state of the church

Meanwhile, the papacy reached a low point. Alexander VI (pope 1492–1503) had several children and used his office to enrich them. Julius II led armies in person. Leo X, pope from 1513, was a cultured and pleasure-loving member of the Medici family, and needed money to rebuild St Peter’s in Rome. The sale of indulgences was the method he chose.

For today

God was at work long before the Reformation broke out. Faithful people prayed, preached and suffered without seeing the outcome. Hus is reported to have said before his death that though they could burn a goose (the meaning of hus in Czech), a swan would come that they could not silence. Our labour in the Lord is not in vain, even when we do not live to see its fruit (1 Corinthians 15:58).

For reflection

Wycliffe, Hus and the Waldensians gave their lives so that ordinary people could read the Bible in their own language. How does that change the way you treat the Bible you own?

7.title: Luther and the German Reformation (1517–1555)
7.essay:
One monk’s search for a gracious God became a movement that changed the church and the world. Luther’s story shows how the recovery of one truth, justification by faith alone, can light a fire no one can put out.

The troubled monk

Martin Luther was born in 1483. In 1505, caught in a thunderstorm, he vowed to become a monk and entered the Augustinian monastery at Erfurt. He threw himself into fasting, prayer and confession, but found no peace. The more he tried, the more he saw that he could not love a God who demanded righteousness he did not have. His superior, Johann von Staupitz, pointed him to Christ and set him to teach the Bible at the new university of Wittenberg.

The righteousness of God

As he lectured on the Psalms, Romans and Galatians, Luther wrestled with the phrase “the righteousness of God” in Romans 1:17. He had understood it as the righteousness by which God punishes sinners. Then he saw that it meant the righteousness God gives freely to those who believe: “For in it the righteousness of God is revealed from faith for faith, as it is written, ‘The righteous shall live by faith’” (Romans 1:17). He later wrote that he felt as if he had been born again and had entered paradise through open gates. Scholars debate exactly when this breakthrough happened, but by 1518 or 1519 it was clear in his teaching.

The Ninety-Five Theses

In 1517 the friar Johann Tetzel was selling indulgences near Wittenberg to raise money for St Peter’s in Rome. He reportedly promised that as soon as the coin rang in the box, a soul sprang out of purgatory. On 31 October 1517 Luther wrote ninety-five theses for debate and sent them to the archbishop. The first said that when Jesus called us to repent, he meant the whole of life to be repentance. The theses were printed and spread across Germany within weeks.

Leipzig and Worms

At the Leipzig Debate in 1519, Johann Eck pushed Luther to admit that popes and councils could err, and that Hus had been right on some points. In 1520 Luther wrote three great tracts. He called on German princes to reform the church, attacked the sacramental system, and described the freedom of the Christian, who is “a perfectly free lord of all, subject to none” by faith, and “a perfectly dutiful servant of all” in love. When the pope’s bull threatening excommunication arrived, Luther burned it.

In 1521 he was summoned before the emperor Charles V at the Diet of Worms and told to recant. He replied that unless he was convinced by Scripture and plain reason, he could not and would not recant, for his conscience was captive to the word of God. The famous words “Here I stand” may have been added later, but they capture the moment.

The Wartburg and the German Bible

On his way home, Luther was “kidnapped” by friends and hidden in the Wartburg castle by his protector, Frederick the Wise, elector of Saxony. There, in about eleven weeks, he translated the New Testament from Erasmus’s Greek into vivid, everyday German. It was published in 1522, and the whole Bible followed in 1534. Luther’s Bible shaped the German language itself.

Reforming the church

Back in Wittenberg, Luther restrained others who wanted to smash images and force change overnight. He preached that the word must do the work. Worship was gradually put into German, with congregational hymns, many written by Luther himself. Monks and nuns left the monasteries. In 1525 Luther married a former nun, Katharina von Bora, and their home became a model of Protestant family life. His Small Catechism of 1529 taught the faith to children and families.

Troubles and divisions

In 1525 the peasants rose in revolt, partly inspired by the language of Christian freedom. Luther first rebuked the lords for their oppression, then urged them to crush the rebels with violence. Many thousands died, and Luther’s harsh words have rightly been criticised. Later in life he also wrote terrible things against the Jews, which later generations, including the Nazis, misused. He was a great servant of God, and a sinner.

In 1529, at Marburg, Luther met the Swiss reformer Zwingli. They agreed on fourteen of fifteen points, but not on the Lord’s Supper. Luther insisted that Christ’s body is truly present in, with and under the bread; Zwingli saw the Supper as a memorial. The Protestant movement remained divided.

Augsburg

In 1530 the Lutheran princes presented the Augsburg Confession, written by Luther’s colleague Philip Melanchthon, to the emperor. It remains the chief Lutheran confession. Luther died in 1546. After years of war, the Peace of Augsburg in 1555 allowed each German prince to choose whether his territory would be Lutheran or Catholic.

For today

Luther’s great discovery is still the heart of the gospel: we are not accepted by God because we have become righteous, but declared righteous because of Christ, received by faith alone. His failings remind us that God uses flawed people, and that heroes are not to be worshipped. But his courage at Worms calls every Christian to have a conscience bound to the word of God.

For reflection

Do you still, like the young Luther, try to make yourself acceptable to God? What would it look like to rest in the righteousness he gives?

8.title: Zwingli, the Anabaptists and Calvin (1519–1619)
8.essay:
Alongside Luther, a second stream of reform rose in Switzerland. It became the Reformed tradition, shaped above all by John Calvin. A third, more radical stream rejected infant baptism and the state church altogether.

Zwingli in Zurich

Ulrich Zwingli became preacher at the Great Minster in Zurich in 1519. Instead of following the set readings, he began preaching straight through Matthew’s Gospel, verse by verse. In 1522 some of his supporters ate sausages during Lent, and Zwingli defended them: Scripture did not forbid it. The city council held public debates and, persuaded by Scripture, reformed the church. The Mass was replaced in 1525 by a simple Lord’s Supper, and images were removed from the churches.

Zwingli stressed that worship must follow what Scripture commands. He saw the Supper chiefly as a memorial and a pledge of faith. He was killed in 1531, fighting with Zurich’s army against the Catholic cantons at the Battle of Kappel. His successor, Heinrich Bullinger, led the Zurich church for over forty years and wrote the Second Helvetic Confession (1566).

The Anabaptists

Some of Zwingli’s own young followers, led by Conrad Grebel and Felix Manz, believed he was moving too slowly. Reading the New Testament, they found no infant baptism, only the baptism of believers. On 21 January 1525, in a house in Zurich, Grebel baptised George Blaurock, and the Anabaptist movement was born. Their enemies called them Anabaptists, meaning “re-baptisers.”

They taught that the church is a gathered community of believers, separate from the state. Most refused to swear oaths, bear arms or serve as magistrates, as set out in the Schleitheim Confession of 1527. Catholics and Protestants alike persecuted them savagely. In 1527 Zurich drowned Felix Manz in the river Limmat. Thousands died across Europe.

In 1534–35 a group of radicals seized the city of Münster, declared it the New Jerusalem, and practised polygamy, until the city was taken and its leaders executed. This disaster blackened the name of all Anabaptists, though most were peaceful. The former priest Menno Simons gathered the scattered communities into the Mennonites. The Baptists of the next century in England arose separately, but shared many of the same convictions about baptism and the church.

Calvin

John Calvin was born in France in 1509 and trained in law. Around 1533 he experienced what he called a sudden conversion, by which God subdued his heart and made it teachable. Forced to flee France, he published the first edition of his Institutes of the Christian Religion in 1536, at the age of twenty-six. He revised it for the rest of his life, until it became the most important systematic theology of the Reformation.

Passing through Geneva in 1536, he was told by the fiery reformer William Farel that God would curse him if he refused to stay. He stayed. Expelled in 1538, he spent three happy years in Strasbourg pastoring French refugees and learning from Martin Bucer. He married Idelette de Bure, a widow. In 1541 he was called back to Geneva, where he worked until his death in 1564.

Geneva

Calvin preached several times a week, usually through whole books of the Bible. He set up the consistory, where pastors and elders together cared for the moral life of the church. He organised care for the poor and the refugees who flooded into the city. In 1559 he founded the Geneva Academy, which trained pastors for France and beyond. Knox called Geneva “the most perfect school of Christ” since the apostles.

There is also a dark page. In 1553 the anti-Trinitarian Michael Servetus was condemned by the city council and burned. Calvin agreed with the verdict, though he asked for a less cruel death. Almost everyone in that age, Catholic and Protestant, believed the state should punish heresy. It was wrong, and we should say so, while remembering that the persecution was not unique to Geneva.

Calvin’s theology

Calvin’s great themes were the glory and sovereignty of God, the authority of Scripture, union with Christ, justification by faith, and the Spirit’s work in sanctification. He taught that Christ is truly present to believers in the Supper by the Spirit, a middle way between Luther and Zwingli. And he taught predestination, not as a cold idea, but as a comfort for believers and a ground for humility.

The Reformed churches spread

The Reformed faith spread to France, the Netherlands, Hungary, Scotland and parts of Germany. In France, the Protestants called Huguenots grew rapidly, but on St Bartholomew’s Day 1572 thousands were massacred in Paris and beyond. In the Netherlands, the Belgic Confession (1561) and the Heidelberg Catechism (1563), from the Palatinate, became standards of faith.

After Calvin’s death, Jacob Arminius, a Dutch professor, questioned unconditional election. His followers, the Remonstrants, set out five points in 1610. The Synod of Dort (1618–1619), with delegates from across the Reformed world, answered them in the Canons of Dort, from which the “five points of Calvinism” come.

For today

The Swiss Reformation teaches us to let Scripture shape not only doctrine, but worship and church life. The Anabaptists, despite their errors, remind us that the church is a community of believers, not a nation. And Calvin’s life shows that deep theology serves the pastoral care of real people. As he put it at the start of the Institutes, true wisdom consists of the knowledge of God and of ourselves.

For reflection

Calvin preached through whole books of the Bible, day after day. How might you let Scripture shape you more steadily and deeply, rather than in fragments?

9.title: Reformation in Britain (1526–1689)
9.essay:
In England the Reformation came by a winding road, through a king’s marriage, a boy king, a Catholic queen and a long struggle over how far reform should go. In Scotland it came more suddenly, through preaching. Together they produced the Puritans and the Westminster Standards.

Tyndale

William Tyndale wanted every ploughboy to know the Scriptures. Forbidden to translate the Bible in England, he went abroad, and in 1526 copies of his English New Testament, translated from the Greek, were smuggled into England in bales of cloth. The bishops bought and burned them, which only paid for more. Tyndale was betrayed in Antwerp, and was strangled and burned in 1536. His last words were said to be a prayer: “Lord, open the king of England’s eyes.” Much of his wording survives in the King James Version.

Henry VIII

Henry VIII wanted to annul his marriage to Catherine of Aragon, who had not given him a son. When the pope refused, Parliament declared Henry Supreme Head of the Church of England in 1534. Henry was no Protestant in doctrine. He broke with Rome but kept much of the old religion. Still, under Thomas Cranmer, archbishop of Canterbury, and Thomas Cromwell, the monasteries were dissolved, and in 1538 an English Bible was ordered to be placed in every parish church.

Edward and Mary

Under Henry’s young son Edward VI (1547–1553) the reform went much further. Cranmer produced the Book of Common Prayer (1549, revised 1552) and the Forty-Two Articles, later revised as the Thirty-Nine Articles, which are clearly Reformed in doctrine. But Edward died at fifteen. His sister Mary (1553–1558) restored Catholicism and burned nearly three hundred Protestants. Hugh Latimer, burning beside Nicholas Ridley in Oxford in 1555, told him to be of good comfort, for by God’s grace they would that day light such a candle in England as would never be put out. Cranmer himself, after recanting under pressure, withdrew his recantation and thrust first into the flames the hand that had signed it.

Elizabeth

Elizabeth I (1558–1603) restored Protestantism, but kept bishops, vestments and much of the old structure. Many who had fled to Geneva and Zurich under Mary came back wanting a fuller reform. They were called Puritans, because they wanted to purify the church. Some stayed within the Church of England; others, called Separatists, left it. Some of these went to Holland, and in 1620 a group sailed to America on the Mayflower.

Knox and Scotland

In Scotland, the preacher George Wishart was burned in 1546. His companion John Knox was captured and spent nineteen months as a galley slave. Later he went to Geneva, and returned to Scotland in 1559. His preaching sparked a revolution. In 1560 the Scottish Parliament rejected the pope’s authority and adopted the Scots Confession. The church was organised along Presbyterian lines, governed by elders rather than bishops. Knox is said to have prayed, “Give me Scotland, or I die.”

The Puritans

The Puritans were above all preachers and pastors. They taught that the whole of life is lived before God: work, marriage, family worship and the Lord’s Day. They wrote deeply about conversion, assurance, suffering and the battle with sin. Richard Sibbes, Thomas Goodwin, John Owen, Richard Baxter, Thomas Watson and John Bunyan are among the best known, and their books are still read.

War and Westminster

James I authorised a new translation, published in 1611, which became known as the King James or Authorised Version. Under his son Charles I, tension grew between the king, with Archbishop Laud, and the Puritan Parliament. Civil war broke out in 1642. In 1643 Parliament called the Westminster Assembly to reform the church. Over six years it produced the Westminster Confession of Faith, the Larger and Shorter Catechisms and a Directory for Public Worship. The Shorter Catechism begins: “What is the chief end of man? Man’s chief end is to glorify God, and to enjoy him for ever.”

Charles I was executed in 1649, and Oliver Cromwell ruled until his death in 1658. Independents like Owen, who believed each congregation should govern itself, adapted the Westminster Confession as the Savoy Declaration in 1658.

The Great Ejection and toleration

When the monarchy was restored in 1660, the new Act of Uniformity (1662) required every minister to accept the whole Prayer Book. About two thousand ministers refused and were ejected from their churches on a single day. Many were imprisoned. Bunyan wrote The Pilgrim’s Progress in prison. Only in 1689, after the Glorious Revolution, did the Act of Toleration allow Protestant dissenters to worship freely. In the same year the Particular Baptists published their confession, closely based on Westminster but holding believer’s baptism. It is known as the 1689 Baptist Confession.

For today

British Christians paid a heavy price for the Bible in English, freedom of conscience and a church shaped by Scripture. The Puritans remind us that doctrine is meant to be lived, in the workplace, the home and the heart. And the ejected ministers remind us that faithfulness can cost a pulpit, a living and a home.

For reflection

Tyndale died so that the ploughboy could read the Bible. What would it take for you to know it better than the scholars who opposed him?

10.title: Rome’s Answer and the Age of Orthodoxy (1540–1700)
10.essay:
The Roman Catholic Church responded to the Reformation with reform of its own and a firm rejection of Protestant teaching. Europe was torn by wars of religion. And Protestants spent the next century defining and defending their faith.

The Jesuits

Ignatius of Loyola, a Spanish soldier, was wounded in 1521 and turned to God while recovering. He founded the Society of Jesus, the Jesuits, approved by the pope in 1540. They were disciplined, highly educated and fiercely loyal to the pope. They founded schools across Europe and won back large parts of Poland, Austria and southern Germany. They were also great missionaries. Francis Xavier took the Roman Catholic faith to India and Japan, and others went to China and the Americas.

The Council of Trent

The Council of Trent met on and off from 1545 to 1563. It reformed abuses: bishops had to live in their dioceses, and seminaries were set up to train priests. But it firmly rejected the Reformation. It declared that Scripture and tradition are to be received with equal reverence, that the Latin Vulgate is the authentic Bible, and that justification includes the inward renewal of the believer, increased by good works. It anathematised anyone who said that a sinner is justified by faith alone. It confirmed the seven sacraments, transubstantiation, the sacrifice of the Mass, and purgatory. Trent’s decrees remain official Roman Catholic teaching today.

The wars of religion

In France, eight wars were fought between Catholics and Huguenots between 1562 and 1598. The Edict of Nantes (1598) gave Protestants limited freedom, but Louis XIV revoked it in 1685, and hundreds of thousands of Huguenots fled abroad.

The Netherlands revolted against Catholic Spain from 1568, under William of Orange, and the northern provinces became a Reformed republic. In Germany, the Thirty Years’ War (1618–1648) began as a religious conflict and became a European power struggle. It devastated Germany, killing perhaps a third of its people in some regions. The Peace of Westphalia in 1648 brought an end to the great wars of religion. Many Europeans came away weary of doctrinal conflict, which helped the rise of the Enlightenment.

Protestant orthodoxy

In this period, Lutheran and Reformed theologians worked to set out their faith in precise, careful detail. This is often called the age of Protestant orthodoxy or Protestant scholasticism. Francis Turretin in Geneva, Johann Gerhard among the Lutherans, and the Westminster divines are examples. They are sometimes accused of turning living faith into cold logic, but more recent scholarship has shown that most were warm-hearted pastors as well. They defended the Reformation against Rome, against the Socinians who denied the Trinity, and against Arminianism.

The Synod of Dort

The Synod of Dort (1618–1619) was the most international Reformed gathering of the age. It answered the five points of the Remonstrants by teaching total depravity, unconditional election, particular redemption, irresistible grace and the perseverance of the saints. Its Canons are careful and pastoral, insisting that election should be preached for the comfort of believers and that no one should despair. With the Belgic Confession and the Heidelberg Catechism they are the Three Forms of Unity, still the confession of many Reformed churches.

Pietism

Towards the end of the century, some Lutherans felt that orthodoxy had become too intellectual. Philipp Jakob Spener’s Pia Desideria (1675) called for Bible study in small groups, a living faith and practical holiness. August Hermann Francke founded schools and an orphanage at Halle. Pietism influenced the Moravians and, through them, John Wesley and the evangelical revivals.

For today

The Council of Trent shows that the disagreement between Rome and the Reformation was not a misunderstanding, but a real difference over how a sinner is made right with God. That difference still matters, and it should be spoken about with truth and charity. The wars of religion warn us never to use the sword for the gospel. And the orthodox and the Pietists together remind us that sound doctrine and warm devotion belong together.

For reflection

Do you lean more towards careful doctrine or warm devotion? What would it look like for both to grow together in you?

11.title: Enlightenment, Revival and Missions (1700–1900)
11.essay:
The eighteenth century put human reason on the throne. Yet in that same century God sent revival on both sides of the Atlantic, and in the century that followed, the gospel went to the ends of the earth.

The Enlightenment

Thinkers of the Enlightenment trusted human reason to discover truth without revelation. Deists believed in a Creator who made the world but did not intervene in it, so miracles, prophecy and the incarnation were set aside. David Hume argued against miracles. In France, Voltaire mocked the church. Many educated people kept a respectable religion of morality, with little place for sin, grace or the cross. The churches of England and Scotland were often cold.

The Moravians

In 1722 a group of refugees descended from the Hussite Brethren settled on the estate of Count Nikolaus von Zinzendorf in Saxony, and founded the village of Herrnhut. In 1727 they experienced a remarkable renewal at a communion service. They began a prayer meeting that continued day and night for about a hundred years. Within decades they were sending missionaries to the West Indies, Greenland and America.

The Great Awakening

In New England, Jonathan Edwards saw revival in Northampton in 1734–35, and again in 1740–42. George Whitefield, a young Anglican preacher, crossed the Atlantic seven times, preaching in the open air to crowds of thousands. Edwards was one of the greatest minds America has produced. He defended the revival against its critics and also warned against its excesses, writing carefully on how to tell true religious affections from false ones.

In England, John Wesley felt his heart “strangely warmed” at a meeting in Aldersgate Street in 1738, while hearing Luther’s preface to Romans read. He and his brother Charles, the great hymn-writer, travelled the country preaching to miners, labourers and the poor. Wesley was Arminian; Whitefield was Calvinist. They disagreed sharply, but remained friends, and Wesley preached at Whitefield’s funeral. Wales and Scotland saw revivals too.

The fruits

The revivals changed Britain. Societies were founded for Bible distribution and Sunday schools. William Wilberforce and the Clapham group of evangelicals fought for decades to end the slave trade, which Parliament abolished in 1807, and slavery itself in the British Empire in 1833. John Newton, a former slave-ship captain, wrote “Amazing Grace” and supported the campaign. Lord Shaftesbury fought for laws to protect children in factories and mines.

The Second Great Awakening

In America, new waves of revival from about 1800 swept the frontier, with camp meetings that drew thousands. Charles Finney (1792–1875) taught that revival was “not a miracle”, but the result of using the right means. He introduced “new measures” such as the anxious bench, where people were called forward to decide. Many were converted, but critics such as the Princeton theologians warned that this approach put the power of salvation in human hands and produced false converts. The debate still shapes evangelism today.

The great century of missions

In 1792 William Carey, a Baptist shoemaker, published his Enquiry into the obligation of Christians to take the gospel to the heathen, and helped found the Baptist Missionary Society. He sailed for India the next year. He translated all or part of the Bible into dozens of languages and campaigned against widow-burning. His motto was, “Expect great things from God; attempt great things for God.”

Many followed. Adoniram and Ann Judson went to Burma in 1813. Robert Moffat and David Livingstone went to Africa. Hudson Taylor founded the China Inland Mission in 1865, adopting Chinese dress and going deep into the interior. Countless missionaries died of disease within months of arriving. By 1900 the church was planted on every continent.

Spurgeon

In London, Charles Haddon Spurgeon (1834–1892) preached to thousands every week at the Metropolitan Tabernacle. He was a Calvinist and a Baptist, and his sermons were printed and read around the world. He founded a college for pastors and an orphanage. Late in life he warned in the Downgrade Controversy that the Baptist Union was drifting from the authority of Scripture, and withdrew from it in 1887.

For today

Revival is God’s work. Edwards called it a “surprising work of God”. But God uses means: prayer, preaching, and ordinary people willing to go. The Moravians prayed; Whitefield preached; Carey went. Every one of us can do at least one of those things. And the debate over Finney reminds us to trust God’s power, not our methods, to change hearts.

For reflection

The Moravian prayer meeting lasted a hundred years. How could you join, in some small way, in praying for revival and for the nations?

12.title: Liberalism, Its Opponents and the Global Church (1800–today)
12.essay:
The last two centuries have seen the faith attacked from within as never before, and spread across the globe as never before. The centre of the church has moved south and east, and the old battles over the Bible still shape us today.

The rise of liberal theology

Friedrich Schleiermacher (1768–1834), often called the father of modern liberal theology, tried to make Christianity attractive to its educated despisers. He located religion in the feeling of absolute dependence, rather than in revealed truth. Others in Germany applied historical criticism to the Bible, treating it as a merely human book. Some questioned whether Moses wrote anything of the Pentateuch, or whether the Gospels tell us much about the real Jesus. In 1859 Charles Darwin published On the Origin of Species, which many took as a reason to doubt the Bible altogether.

By 1900 liberal theology dominated many universities and seminaries. It tended to present Jesus as a great moral teacher, the kingdom of God as social progress, and sin as ignorance. One critic summed it up: a God without wrath brought men without sin into a kingdom without judgment through the ministrations of a Christ without a cross.

The defenders

At Princeton Seminary, Charles Hodge, A. A. Hodge and B. B. Warfield defended the inspiration and inerrancy of Scripture and the Reformed faith. In the Netherlands, Abraham Kuyper founded the Free University of Amsterdam, and Herman Bavinck wrote his great Reformed Dogmatics. Kuyper famously declared that there is not a square inch of human existence over which Christ does not cry, “Mine!”

In America in the 1920s the struggle became the fundamentalist–modernist controversy. J. Gresham Machen’s Christianity and Liberalism (1923) argued that liberalism was not a version of Christianity, but a different religion. When Princeton was reorganised in 1929, Machen and others founded Westminster Theological Seminary, and later the Orthodox Presbyterian Church.

War and the Confessing Church

The First World War shattered liberal optimism about human progress. Karl Barth, a Swiss pastor, turned back to the God who speaks, though his view of Scripture was not that of the Reformers. When Hitler took power in Germany, many Protestants supported the pro-Nazi “German Christians.” In 1934 the Barmen Declaration, largely written by Barth, confessed that Jesus Christ is the one word of God whom we must hear and obey. Dietrich Bonhoeffer, a leader of the Confessing Church, was hanged in 1945 for his part in the resistance.

Pentecostalism

The Azusa Street revival in Los Angeles in 1906 marked the start of the modern Pentecostal movement, with its emphasis on speaking in tongues and spiritual gifts. The charismatic movement later spread these emphases into other churches. Pentecostal and charismatic Christians are now a very large part of the worldwide church, especially in Africa, Latin America and Asia. Reformed Christians differ from them on the continuation of certain gifts, but should honour their zeal for evangelism and prayer.

Rome and the evangelicals

The Second Vatican Council (1962–65) brought major changes in Roman Catholic worship, including the Mass in local languages, and a warmer tone towards other Christians. But it did not withdraw the teaching of Trent. Among evangelicals, Billy Graham preached to millions. The Lausanne Congress of 1974 called evangelicals to world evangelisation. The Chicago Statement on Biblical Inerrancy (1978) restated the classic view of Scripture.

In Britain, Martyn Lloyd-Jones at Westminster Chapel, and the Banner of Truth Trust, revived interest in the Puritans and Reformed theology. John Stott and J. I. Packer served the worldwide evangelical movement. In recent decades there has been a widespread renewal of Reformed theology, especially among younger Christians.

The persecuted church

The twentieth century produced more Christian martyrs than any before it. Under communism in the Soviet Union, Eastern Europe and China, churches were closed and believers imprisoned. Yet the church in China grew from under a million Protestants in 1949 to many millions today. Christians still face severe persecution in parts of the Middle East, Africa and Asia.

The global church

In 1900 most Christians lived in Europe and North America. Today most live in Africa, Latin America and Asia. The church in the West has declined, while churches in the global South are growing and sending missionaries back to Europe. The faith that began in the Middle East has come full circle, a truly worldwide family.

For today

The battles of the last two centuries are not over. The authority of Scripture, the reality of sin, the deity of Christ, his substitutionary death and bodily resurrection are still under attack, often from within the church. Machen’s warning still stands: a gospel emptied of these truths is no gospel at all. Yet Christ is still building his church, faster in some places than ever. The story is not finished, and we are part of it.

For reflection

“Jesus Christ is the same yesterday and today and forever” (Hebrews 13:8). How does the long story of his faithfulness give you courage for the battles of your own day?
